title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Pond and water-feature maintenance
audience: Solo operators and team owners of pond and water-feature maintenance businesses who want more work from clients that suit their service, their area and their route.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a water-feature need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide what work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Targeted search starts with a clear picture of the work you want more of. Write down the water features you service well, such as backyard ponds, koi ponds, garden water features and small commercial fountains, the price range you can sustain, the suburbs you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each kind of client needs you. A monthly visit on a route you already run is worth far more to a small business than a single large clean-out across town. These criteria are the filter for everything that follows.

instruction.heading: Build a scored prospect list
instruction.body: Keep every candidate in one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, using the written criteria. Ask whether it sits inside your service area, whether it has a repeat need, whether you can reach the person who decides, and whether the work falls within the licence and insurance you hold. Landscapers and garden designers can be partners rather than prospects. Pet and aquarium retailers are a possible referral route, because Queensland's fact sheet says unwanted fish go back to the retailer, to a new home, or are humanely destroyed (Queensland DAF, June 2020). Body corporate committees with a water feature in common property, and councils that run water features, are segments to score. Add a prospect only when it passes the criteria. Business.gov.au suggests a short profile for each segment (24 September 2024). Keep only business contact details that are published for business use. Do not use bought or harvested contact lists, because buying a list does not remove the need to show consent (ACMA, Spam Act obligations, 28 March 2019).

instruction.heading: Watch for signals that a water-feature need is starting
instruction.body: A signal is a public event that makes a need more likely soon. Examples include a public tender for maintenance of a council water feature, a body corporate notice of planned works to a common-area pond, and a new commercial fit-out with a water feature. Use signals to decide when to make contact, not to build a profile of individuals. Do not monitor private people, do not use personal information that is not public, and do not turn up at a home to make an offer. In Victoria, Buying for Victoria lists current and past tenders, and suppliers can set alerts (last updated 7 August 2026). Each state and territory runs its own tender system for local government and state work (business.gov.au, 19 August 2025). Some councils publish planning permit registers, such as the City of Casey register on the Victorian open-data portal, so check whether your own council publishes one. The research did not find a public signal specific to ponds, so treat these as general signals to test.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A useful first message does three things. It says how you came to know about the business or the work. It makes one specific observation that you can check from public view or from the business's own published material, such as a notice about works at a common-area pond. It then offers one small next step, such as a written quote for a defined area or a fifteen-minute call. Keep the message short, do not overstate what you know, and make it simple to say no. The ACCC's 2026 review of unsolicited selling found many approaches were pressured or misleading, and many salespeople did not identify themselves (28 July 2026). A specific, honest message that names you is therefore a practical advantage as well as a compliance step. If the message offers fish rehoming, check that the state rule allows the arrangement before you send it.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide in advance how many follow-ups you will send and how far apart they will be. A common pattern is one reminder after a week and one final message after a further two weeks, followed by a pause. If a prospect says no, or asks you to stop, remove them from the list at once and record the request with its date. At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced the replies that became paid work, and move your effort toward them.

procedure: Write the water-feature type, area, price and repeat-need criteria for the work you want.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason.
Choose two or three public signals to watch and note the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules, the do-not-call rules for any call, and the licence and fish rules for the work before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of the month.

workedExamples.situation: A pond business covers three suburbs in Victoria. A tender notice appears for the maintenance of several ornamental water features in public parks, and it closes in four weeks. A body corporate in one suburb also posts a notice about planned works to a common-area pond, with a building manager's business email on the notice.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which opportunity should the owner act on first, and what should the first step be?
workedExamples.reasoning: The tender is a public, published opportunity, and the owner can look up the scope, the closing date and any alert the portal offers. Before responding, the owner confirms the scope, capacity and deadline, as Business Queensland advises before sending a quote, and checks that the owner holds the insurance the scope needs. The body corporate notice is a signal about a business that has published its own contact details, but publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages (ACMA). The owner does not send a sales email to the building manager unless the manager has invited contact or agreed to receive messages, and checks the Do Not Call Register before any phone call. The owner does not contact individual owners or tenants, and does not enter the common area without an invitation.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, water-feature type and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list at once.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about an individual to make contact.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Pitching fish rehoming or relocation that the state rule does not allow.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the rule for the state before outreach, and remove that service from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a licensed or authorised service in outreach unless you hold the licence that the state where the work is done requires. No pond or water-feature licence was confirmed in any state. This lesson does not grant any licence.

Fish rules are state-based. Releasing fish into New South Wales public waters without a permit is illegal. In Victoria, koi need a permit to keep, transport, sell or possess. Do not offer koi relocation or release in outreach until the state rule has been checked.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA's guidance says marketing messages need consent, that consent should be recorded, and that unsubscribe requests must be honoured within five working days (read 2026-11-03). ACMA's Spam Act obligations page (last updated 28 March 2019) says publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages. The Act text was not read for this lesson.

Information on a public listing or a public notice does not by itself permit contact about anything. If the Privacy Act applies to your business, the OAIC's guidance on direct marketing (APP 7, version dated 22 July 2019) says that public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules. Use only contact details published for business use, keep them secure, and stop using them when someone objects.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added.
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen.
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned.
summary: Define the water-feature work you want first, then filter prospects against that definition.
Watch public signals, and never use private information to make contact.
Keep the first approach specific and easy to decline, and stop when asked.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should a pond business contact first?
options: A one-off pond a long way outside your service area, because it looks large
A body corporate with several water features inside your service area that you already visit
Any business that has a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A public notice shows planned works at a common-area pond in your area. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Contact the building's manager about the works, by a route that the electronic message and do-not-call rules allow
Message each owner using their private contact details and ask them to sign up for your pond service
Go into the common area to look at the pond before making contact and ask the crew what they are doing

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Check that the message is short enough to read on a phone and it has a fun subject line
Ask the prospect to like your social media page first and then send the message
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance before sending

Gap: no pond-specific prospect, signal or referral figure was found. No pond licence or trade-body source was found. Do Not Call Register telemarketing hours were not restated here; check the current DNCR guide before calling.

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam (ACMA)
officialReferences.covers: Read 2026-11-03: marketing messages need consent, and consent must be recorded; each message must identify the sender and include correct contact details; every commercial message must include an unsubscribe option honoured within five working days. Does not cover privacy law. Publisher: ACMA.

officialReferences.title: Australian Privacy Principles guidelines (OAIC)
officialReferences.covers: Read 2026-11-03: the APPs apply to organisations covered by the Privacy Act, which the page says covers organisations with an annual turnover of more than $3 million and some other organisations. Small-business coverage and consent detail are unconfirmed here. Publisher: OAIC.
